title: Kernel and Range
body:
Two subspaces attached to a [[Linear Transformation]] $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ with
matrix $A$. **The kernel is what $T$ destroys; the range is what $T$ can produce.**

Not to be confused with the operating system [[Kernel]] in Computing Machinery. Same word, unrelated
concept.

## Kernel

$$
\ker T = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n : T(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{0}\}
$$

Everything sent to zero. Also called the **null space** of $A$, and it is precisely the solution
set of the homogeneous [[System of Linear Equations]] $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$, which is why
those systems get their own treatment. It is a subspace **of the domain**, and it always
contains $\mathbf{0}$.

Its dimension is the **nullity**. To find a [[Basis]] for it: row reduce, and read off one basis
vector per free variable.

$\ker T = \{\mathbf{0}\}$ exactly when $T$ is **one-to-one**. The argument is short and worth
keeping: if $T(\mathbf{u}) = T(\mathbf{v})$ then $T(\mathbf{u}-\mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{0}$, so a
trivial kernel forces $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v}$. **A linear map collapses things exactly when it
collapses something to zero**, which is not true of functions in general and is a real
convenience.

## Range

$$
\text{range}\,T = \{T(\mathbf{x}) : \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^n\}
$$

Everything actually hit. Also called the **image**, or the **column space** of $A$, and that
second name is the useful one: by the column reading in [[Matrix Multiplication]], $A\mathbf{x}$
is a combination of $A$'s columns, so the range **is** the span of the columns. It is a subspace
**of the codomain**.

Its dimension is the **rank**. To find a basis: row reduce and take the *original* columns
sitting in pivot positions.

$A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ is consistent exactly when $\mathbf{b}$ lies in the range. So the two
subspaces answer the two halves of the solving question: the range decides whether a solution
exists, the kernel decides whether it is unique.

## Rank-nullity

$$
\text{rank}(A) + \text{nullity}(A) = n
$$

with $n$ the number of **columns**, which is the dimension of the domain. Every input dimension
is either preserved into the range or crushed into the kernel, and nothing goes missing.

Example: projection onto the $x$-axis in $\mathbb{R}^2$ has rank $1$ (the range is the $x$-axis)
and nullity $1$ (the kernel is the $y$-axis), summing to $2$.

Consequences the course leans on:

- $\text{rank}(A) \leq \min(m, n)$. **Full rank** means it hits that bound.
- For square $A$: rank $n$ means nullity $0$, means trivial kernel, means invertible. Another
  row of the equivalence table in [[Matrix Inverse]], and now it has a geometric meaning.
- $n > m$ (more unknowns than equations) forces nullity $\geq n - m > 0$, so a non-trivial kernel
  is guaranteed. That is the earlier claim that a wide homogeneous system always has non-trivial
  solutions, now with a reason.
- Row rank equals column rank, always, which is not obvious and is why "rank" needs no
  qualifier.

## Why rank is the useful number

Rank is **how much information a matrix actually carries**, as opposed to how big it is. A
$1000 \times 1000$ matrix of rank $3$ describes a three-dimensional situation stored wastefully,
and finding that out is the point of [[Low-Rank Approximation]] and dimensionality reduction. That
line of thinking runs from here through the [[Singular Value Decomposition]] into
[[Principal Component Analysis]], which is
[[LINEAR ALGEBRA FOR DATA SCIENCE]]'s material and the vault's route into
[[MACHINE LEARNING]].
